title: Reading strengths from labels: mg/5 mL, mg in 1 mL, mg/2 mL, units/mL
blurb: Read what a label's strength really means, find the amount per mL or per container, and pick the right numbers for want ÷ have.
question: An ampoule is labelled 100 mg/2 mL. A colleague says each mL contains 100 mg. Are they right, and how much is in 1 mL?

teach.h: The strength is a pair of numbers
teach.body: A label strength gives an amount AND the volume that contains it: 250 mg/5 mL means 250 mg in every 5 mL. Plain English: the "have" in your formula is the first number, and the stock volume is the second. Do not drop the second number: 100 mg/2 mL is 50 mg in each mL, not 100. On Part A the label is a picture; our stems print the strength in words.
teach.cite: FACTS section 1: labels carry the numbers

teach.body: The strength (concentration) is not the same as the total in the container. A 2 mL ampoule labelled 50 mg/mL holds 100 mg in total; a 100 mL bottle of 250 mg/5 mL holds 5000 mg. Read whether a label gives "per mL" or "per ampoule" before you use it.

teach.h: Worked example: learning disability community team
items: Community nurse Olu Adebayo supports a client prescribed sodium valproate 300 mg. The bottle label reads 200 mg/5 mL.
Per-mL check: 200 ÷ 5 = 40 mg per mL; 7.5 x 40 = 300 mg.
Sense check: more than 200 mg, so more than 5 mL.

teach.text: Treating "mg/2 mL" or "mg/5 mL" as if it were "per 1 mL" halves or fifths the volume you give: 75 mg from 100 mg/2 mL becomes 0.75 mL instead of 1.5 mL. Always carry the label's own volume into the formula.

items: A strength is an amount in a volume: use both numbers.
Have = the amount; stock volume = the volume it is in.
Per mL = amount ÷ volume; total = per mL x container volume.
Units, mmol and micrograms read the same way as mg.
Check the label volume before using want ÷ have.

summary: You can now read a label strength as an amount in a volume, work out the amount per mL and the total in a container, and put the right numbers into want ÷ have x volume.

A.q: An oral suspension is labelled 125 mg/5 mL. How many milligrams are in each 1 mL?

whyNot.1: This is the amount in 5 mL, not in 1 mL.
whyNot.3: Divided 5 by 125; divide the amount by the volume.

A.q: An ampoule is labelled 100 mg/2 mL. How many milligrams are in each 1 mL?

whyNot.2: This is the amount in 2 mL, not in 1 mL.
whyNot.3: Divided 2 by 100; divide the amount by the volume.

A.q: A 30 mL bottle of oral solution is labelled 5 mg/5 mL. How many milligrams are in the whole bottle?
A.why: 5 mg/5 mL = 1 mg per mL. 30 mL x 1 mg = 30 mg.

whyNot.0: Multiplied 5 mg by 30 mL; the strength is per 5 mL, not per 1 mL.
whyNot.1: Divided 30 by 5 and stopped; that is the number of 5 mL lots.
whyNot.2: This is the amount in 5 mL, not the whole bottle.

B.q: A person on a mental health ward is prescribed flupentixol decanoate 40 mg by depot injection. The ampoule is labelled 100 mg/mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.3: Gave the dose in mg as the volume.

B.q: A client with a learning disability is prescribed sodium valproate 300 mg. The oral solution is labelled 200 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.2: Treated the label as 200 mg per 1 mL.
whyNot.3: Divided 300 by 5 instead of using the 200 mg strength.

B.q: A newborn baby is prescribed vitamin K 1 mg IM. The ampoule is labelled 2 mg/0.2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
B.why: 1 ÷ 2 x 0.2 = 0.1 mL. The label is 10 mg per mL.

whyNot.0: This is the whole ampoule, which contains 2 mg.
whyNot.1: Read the label as 1 mg per mL.

C.q: An adult is prescribed 200 mg by injection. The ampoules are labelled 80 mg/2 mL. What total volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: Treated the label as 80 mg per 1 mL.
whyNot.3: Drew up three whole 2 mL ampoules, which is 240 mg.

C.q: A woman is prescribed oxytocin 5 units by slow IV injection. The ampoule is labelled 10 units/mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: Gave the dose in units as the volume.

C.q: A person is prescribed 25 mmol of an oral electrolyte solution. The label reads 2 mmol/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.2: Read the label as 1 mmol per mL.

reteach.title: Say the label out loud
reteach.question: How would you read "80 mg/2 mL" as a sentence?

blocks.body: Say every label as "X in every Y": "80 milligrams in every 2 millilitres". Spoken that way, the volume cannot be forgotten. Then halve, quarter or divide to reach 1 mL if that helps: 80 in every 2 is 40 in every 1.

blocks.text: A label with a volume other than 1 mL is the commonest place to lose a factor of 2 or 5.

explain.body: Amount in any volume = (label amount ÷ label volume) x volume.

test.q: An oral liquid is labelled 200 mg/5 mL. How many milligrams are in 2 mL?

whyNot.2: This is the amount in 1 mL.
whyNot.3: Divided 200 by 2 and multiplied by 5: the volumes are swapped.

explain.body: Divide the amount by 2 to get per mL.

test.q: An ampoule is labelled 40 mg/2 mL. How many milligrams are in each 1 mL?

whyNot.1: This is the amount in 2 mL.
whyNot.2: Divided 2 by 40; divide the amount by the volume.

explain.body: Total = amount per mL x container volume.

test.q: An ampoule labelled 50 mg/mL holds 2 mL. How many milligrams are in the whole ampoule?

whyNot.1: This is the amount in 1 mL.
whyNot.3: Added the volume to the strength.

explain.body: Scale up to 1 mL: 5000 units in 0.2 mL is 5 x 5000 per 1 mL.

test.q: A prefilled syringe is labelled 5,000 units/0.2 mL. How many units are in each 1 mL?

whyNot.1: This is the amount in 0.2 mL.
